title: Synthesis and Characterization of Cationic and Non-Ionic Surfactant Added Organomodified Montmorillonite and the Effect on Migration Characteristics for Starch-Based Film Materials.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
Preparation of Film Materials
sections.text: 2.3.1 Preparation of Film Materials To ensure film flexibility, glycerol was added as a plasticizer to the film‐forming solution to keep water molecules within polymer; the resulting matrix is known as thermoplastic starch (TPS) (Agarwal  2021 ). First, the amount of glycerol was determined on the basis of preliminary studies conducted without incorporation of nanofiller in structure. Starch was first dried in oven at 70°C for approximately 12 h to remove free water (Aouada et al.  2011 ). Glycerol was added to starch at varying dry weight ratios (30%, 40%, 50%, and 60% w/w, based on starch) and dissolved by mixing in water using a magnetic stirrer with a heating plate. Then, the mixture was poured into a Petri dish and dried at 30°C ± 2°C for 15 h. The quantity of plasticizer has a significant impact on macroscopic properties of starch‐based films (Agarwal  2021 ). The film material containing 40% glycerol ensured good processability and formation of uniform structure, with this concentration yielding the most favorable results in terms of overall appearance, exhibiting desirable macroscopic characteristics, such as smoothness, non‐brittleness, rigidity, sturdiness, flexibility, non‐sticky surface upon handling, and ease of detachment from the Petri dish. Starch nanocomposite films were subsequently produced by solvent casting method, as shown in Figure  2 . The preparation procedure for biocomposite materials was modified on the basis of techniques outlined by Aouada et al. ( 2011 ) and Suryanto et al. ( 2019 ). Dried starch (5.0% w/v, based on final volume of solution) and glycerol (40% w/w, based on starch) were weighed and mixed with 50 mL of ultrapure water. The mixture was stirred using a magnetic stirrer for 1 h at room temperature (Mixture A). Clay concentration in the matrix was studied at levels of 3% and 5% (w/w, based on starch). A known quantity of organoclay and surfactant‐free clay was weighed, and 50 mL of ultrapure water was added (Mixture B). Mixture B was stirred for 16 h at room temperature on a magnetic stirrer, then ultrasonic treatment (35 kHz, 860 W, 60 min) was performed in an ultrasonic bath (Sonorex RK514BH, BANDELIN Electronic GmbH & Co. KG, Berlin, Germany) to prevent agglomeration of clay in the biocomposite material and to ensure homogeneous distribution. Mixtures A and B were then combined and stirred for 1 h at room temperature. As control film (S), starch and glycerol were weighed, and 100 mL of ultrapure water was put in without adding clay/organoclay, followed by stirring for 2 h. After stirring for 20 min at gelatinization temperature (65–70°C), 25 mL of film‐forming solution was cast onto Petri dishes (90 × 17 mm 2 ) and allowed to dry at 30°C ± 2°C for 24 h in oven. The dried films were removed from Petri dishes and kept in a desiccator until measurements were conducted. The thickness of film materials was 0.187 ± 0.017 mm. FIGURE 2 The scheme of the procedure to prepare starch‐based nanocomposite film materials.

operations.sentence: Due to the hydrophilic structure of Mt clay, it was placed in drying oven (Universal UF110, Memmert GmbH + Co.KG, Schwabach, Germany) at 80°C for 12 h prior to use.
Subsequently, surfactant was added, and the mixture was stirred with magnetic stirrer (RT15 power, IKA‐Werke GmbH & Co. KG, Staufen, Germany) at room temperature.
Treated Mt suspension was centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 10 min using centrifuge (Universal 320R, Andreas Hettich GmbH & Co. KG, Tuttlingen, Germany).
The settled part was repeatedly washed with ultrapure water and centrifuged to eliminate excess surfactant from the surface of modified clays.
The material was then dried in oven at 80°C for 24 h, followed by grinding using mortar and grinder (Aromatic, Fakir Hausgeräte GmbH, Vaihingen/Enz, Germany).
As control (blank), nanoclay (Mt, unmodified/surfactant‐free clay) was dispersed in ultrapure water without adding any surfactant, and the same procedure was followed.

2.3 Starch‐Based Nanocomposite Film Materials 2.3.1 Preparation of Film Materials To ensure film flexibility, glycerol was added as a plasticizer to the film‐forming solution to keep water molecules within polymer; the resulting matrix is known as thermoplastic starch (TPS) (Agarwal  2021 ).
Starch was first dried in oven at 70°C for approximately 12 h to remove free water (Aouada et al.  2011 ).
Glycerol was added to starch at varying dry weight ratios (30%, 40%, 50%, and 60% w/w, based on starch) and dissolved by mixing in water using a magnetic stirrer with a heating plate.
Then, the mixture was poured into a Petri dish and dried at 30°C ± 2°C for 15 h.
Dried starch (5.0% w/v, based on final volume of solution) and glycerol (40% w/w, based on starch) were weighed and mixed with 50 mL of ultrapure water.
The mixture was stirred using a magnetic stirrer for 1 h at room temperature (Mixture A).
A known quantity of organoclay and surfactant‐free clay was weighed, and 50 mL of ultrapure water was added (Mixture B).

Mixture B was stirred for 16 h at room temperature on a magnetic stirrer, then ultrasonic treatment (35 kHz, 860 W, 60 min) was performed in an ultrasonic bath (Sonorex RK514BH, BANDELIN Electronic GmbH & Co. KG, Berlin, Germany) to prevent agglomeration of clay in the biocomposite material and to ensure homogeneous distribution.
Mixtures A and B were then combined and stirred for 1 h at room temperature.
As control film (S), starch and glycerol were weighed, and 100 mL of ultrapure water was put in without adding clay/organoclay, followed by stirring for 2 h.
After stirring for 20 min at gelatinization temperature (65–70°C), 25 mL of film‐forming solution was cast onto Petri dishes (90 × 17 mm 2 ) and allowed to dry at 30°C ± 2°C for 24 h in oven.
The dried films were removed from Petri dishes and kept in a desiccator until measurements were conducted.

At the end of test period, test samples were removed from water; surface water was gently dried with filter paper and weighed to obtain wet weight ( W W 
 ).
The materials that are suspected to contain water‐soluble components should be reconditioned for same test conditions as the initial drying process after immersion in ultrapure water.
Swollen samples from water absorption capacity test were dried at 50°C ± 2°C for 24 h in an oven for reconditioning.
First, clean glass Petri dishes were labeled for identification and placed in an oven at 105–110°C to dry for 60 min.
This step of the procedure was carried out in the minimum time possible to avoid unnecessary heat loss.
Each container that contained food simulant was rinsed with two portions of 10 mL of fresh simulant, and the evaporation process was continued.
When the simulant had evaporated, glass dishes were placed in the oven at 105–110°C for 60 min to complete the evaporation process and dry any remaining residue.
